raw_case_text:
The patient was a 28-year-old male, resident in Fortaleza, Ceara State and was admitted in the emergency room of Sao Jose Hospital of Infectious Diseases in May 2017. The symptoms had started 5 days prior to admission with fever, adynamia, myalgia, and worsening of general condition. He denied retroorbital pain, bleeding phenomena or abdominal pain. He had taken no medications in the previous year and had not traveled outside of Brazil. There was no previous history of cardiopathies.
Upon the initial examination, the Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score of the patient was E4 V5 M6. He had a heart rate of 120 beats per minute and had hypotension (70/40 mm of Hg). There was no heart murmur or pericardial rub and his pulmonary examination was unremarkable. The skin showed no rashes, and there were no petechiae or jaundice.
The electrocardiogram (EKG) showed supraventricular tachycardia (230 bpm) not responsive to intravenous adenosine. An electric cardioversion was performed and successfully restored the normal heart rhythm. A new EKG was performed showing ST elevation with upper concavity and PR segment depression in DII, DIII and aVF, such as ST depression in V1 and aVR. The patient was then admitted to the intensive care unit. His laboratory parameters are described in Table 1. A first transthoracic echocardiogram revealed an altered left ventricular ejection fraction (EF) (43%), left ventricular hypercontractility, and mild bilateral pericardial and pleural effusions (Figure 1). After 5 days, a new echocardiogram was performed, revealing a 36.4% EF, as well as diffuse hypokinesia and moderate pericardial effusion.
Dobutamine (2.9 mcg/Kg/min) IV was initiated and maintained for 4 days and a single dose of 400 mg of hydrocortisone IV was administered. Treatments with immunoglobulin IV or colchicine were not considered. Paired blood cultures were negative for pyogenic agents. Antibiotics were not used.
Serologies for coxsackie virus, rubella, Chagas disease, human immunodeficiency virus, cytomegalovirus, Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), toxoplasmosis, hepatitis B virus and hepatitis C virus were negative. The patient's serum samples were tested and found to be ELISA-IgM positive and ELISA-IgG positive for DENV and ELISA-IgM positive for CHIKV. The DENV NS1 antigen test yielded a negative result. There was a good response to therapy and the patient progressed with gradual improvement until recovery of ventricular function. After 11 days, a last echocardiogram showed an EF of 70% and persistence of pericardial effusion. The patient was discharged from the hospital 11 days after admission. Table 1 shows laboratory results during hospital stay.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 28-year-old male presenting with fever, adynamia, myalgia, and worsening general condition for five days.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 28-year-old male presented with a 5-day history of fever, adynamia, myalgia, and deterioration of general condition. Upon arrival to the emergency unit, he presented in shock with supraventricular tachycardia refractory to intravenous adenosine, requiring emergent synchronized electrical cardioversion to restore normal sinus rhythm, followed by transfer to the intensive care unit.
subjective.past_medical_history: No previous history of cardiopathies; no medications taken in the previous year. Epidemiological history: Resident of Fortaleza, Ceará State, Brazil; no travel history outside Brazil.
subjective.review_of_systems: Denies retroorbital pain, abdominal pain, or bleeding phenomena.

objective.physical_examination: Glasgow Coma Scale score 15 (E4 V5 M6). Heart rate 120 beats/min, blood pressure 70/40 mmHg (hypotension). Cardiovascular: No heart murmurs or pericardial rub. Respiratory: Pulmonary examination unremarkable. Dermatologic: Absence of cutaneous rashes, petechiae, or jaundice.
objective.routine_investigations: EKG on admission: Supraventricular tachycardia (230 bpm) unresponsive to intravenous adenosine; post-cardioversion EKG revealed ST-segment elevation with upper concavity and PR-segment depression in leads DII, DIII, and aVF, with reciprocal ST depression in V1 and aVR. Bedside transthoracic echocardiogram (day 1): Altered left ventricular ejection fraction (EF 43%), left ventricular hypercontractility, and mild bilateral pericardial and pleural effusions; repeat echocardiogram at day 5 showed EF 36.4%, diffuse hypokinesia, and moderate pericardial effusion; follow-up echocardiogram at day 11 showed recovery of left ventricular systolic function with EF 70% and persistence of pericardial effusion. Paired blood cultures: Negative for pyogenic agents. Serologies negative for coxsackievirus, rubella, Chagas disease, HIV, cytomegalovirus, Epstein-Barr virus, toxoplasmosis, hepatitis B virus, and hepatitis C virus.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Confirmed Dengue virus (DENV) infection complicated by acute viral myocarditis, cardiogenic shock, supraventricular tachycardia, and pericardial/pleural effusions, with serological reactivity/coinfection for Chikungunya virus. Confirmatory testing showed serum ELISA-IgM and ELISA-IgG positive for DENV and ELISA-IgM positive for CHIKV, while DENV NS1 antigen test was negative. Paired blood cultures were negative for bacterial pathogens, and serologies for coxsackievirus, rubella, Chagas disease, HIV, CMV, EBV, toxoplasmosis, HBV, and HCV were negative.
Plan & Outcome: Emergent electrical cardioversion successfully restored sinus rhythm. Hemodynamics supported with intravenous dobutamine (2.9 mcg/kg/min) for 4 days, alongside a single dose of intravenous hydrocortisone 400 mg. Intravenous immunoglobulin, colchicine, and antibiotics were not administered. The patient exhibited gradual clinical recovery and normalization of left ventricular function (EF improved to 70%), and was discharged in stable condition 11 days after admission.
